title: Note down who came before
allegory: A previous-token head is like everyone in a queue glancing at the person just in front and sticking that name on a note on their own back, so a later searcher can ask 'who stood behind Alice?' and find the answer.
map: glancing at the person just in front
writing that name on a note on your own back
writing 'the token before me was X' into position i's residual stream
a later searcher hunting for the note that says 'Alice'
an induction head's keys reading that subspace (K-composition)
the note never answers anything by itself
its effect is indirect, so direct logit attribution scores it near zero

props.label: who was in front of me?

cap.1: To guess what comes next, it helps to know what came just before. But each word starts out knowing only itself and its place in line.
cap.2: At the start of the stream, each position holds only its own token and position embedding. To use 'the token before me', some head has to fetch it.
cap.3: x₀ at position i encodes only (tokenᵢ, i). Previous-token information has to be moved across positions by attention, the only cross-position operation.

cap.1: In a queue, everyone glances at the person just in front and writes that name on a note stuck to their own back. That is the whole job.
cap.2: A previous-token head at position i attends almost entirely to position i−1, then writes 'the token before me was X' into position i's residual stream.
cap.3: Pattern: A[i, i−1] ≈ 1, a bright sub-diagonal. The OV circuit then writes a representation of token_{i−1} into resid at i, in a subspace later heads can read.

chapters.name: The stripe
chapters.title: Attention pattern of a previous-token head (illustrative)

cap.1: Each row is a word looking back. Almost all of its attention lands on the word just before it: a bright stripe one step below the diagonal.
cap.2: Rows are destinations, columns are sources. A previous-token head lights up the sub-diagonal. Your detector: average pattern.diagonal(-1) and flag heads above a threshold.
cap.3: Score = mean of A.diagonal(offset=−1) over positions. Offset 0 would flag current-token heads; offset 1 − seq_len on repeated text flags induction heads.

cap.1: Later, A shows up again. A second head searches the queue for a note saying 'A was in front of me', finds B, and guesses B comes next.
cap.2: The induction head's keys read the note the previous-token head wrote. That is K-composition: the first head decides where the second one looks.
cap.3: In ARENA's 2-layer attention-only model, head 0.7 is the prev-token head and 1.4 and 1.10 are induction heads; ablate 0.7 and loss on repeated text climbs back up.

chapters.name: Invisible to DLA
chapters.verdict: The pattern suggests the role; patching proves it.

cap.1: The note on Bob's back never shouts an answer itself, so counting who spoke up misses it. To prove it matters, peel the note off and see who gets lost.
cap.2: Direct logit attribution scores a prev-token head near zero, because it only helps through later heads. Ablate or patch it and watch induction fail.
cap.3: DLA sees only direct paths, and the prev-token head's effect is entirely indirect via K-composition. [1.4.1] validates the IOI circuit's prev-token heads by patching.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The first half of every induction circuit
Quiet heads can matter through others

cap.1: Many clever behaviours are relays: one simple head leaves a note, another uses it. Finding the note-writers is how you see how a model really works.
cap.2: Previous-token heads feed induction heads, which Anthropic tied to in-context learning. To understand or edit that behaviour you have to find the quiet first half too.
cap.3: Composition makes importance non-local: a component with zero direct effect can be necessary. Circuit discovery needs causal interventions, not only direct attribution.

coda.title: Write your own detector: draw where each word looks

readouts.label: previous-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.slice(1).map((row, k) => { const s = sum(row.slice(0, k + 2)); return s > 0 ? row[k] / s : 0; })).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: current-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.map((row, i) => { const s = sum(row.slice(0, i + 1)); return s > 0 ? row[i] / s : 0; })).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: first-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.map((row, i) => { const s = sum(row.slice(0, i + 1)); return s > 0 ? row[0] / s : 0; })).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: detector says
readouts.f: (() => { const n = G.map((row, i) => { const s = sum(row.slice(0, i + 1)); return row.map((v, j) => j <= i && s > 0 ? v / s : 0); }); const p = mean(n.slice(1).map((row, k) => row[k])); const c = mean(n.map((row, i) => row[i])); const f = mean(n.map(row => row[0])); const b = Math.max(p, c, f); return b < 0.4 ? 'no clear role' : b === p ? 'previous-token head' : b === c ? 'current-token head' : 'first-token head'; })()

caption.1: Tap cells to draw where each word looks. Rows only look left, never right. Keep the stripe just below the diagonal and the detector names a previous-token head.
caption.2: This is the detector you write in [1.2]: normalise each row, then average the sub-diagonal, the diagonal, or column 0. Now try drawing a current-token or first-token head.
caption.3: Scores are mean A[i, i−1], A[i, i] and A[i, 0] over causal, row-normalised patterns. Detectors are heuristics that flag candidates; ablation or patching confirms roles.

where_else: The first half of every induction circuit

Bigram-style prediction: knowing the previous word is the simplest basis for guessing the next
Shift registers and causal convolutions, which pass each value one step along

hamming.what: An attention head that looks one position back and writes the previous token's identity into the current position.
hamming.when: Early in the model, wherever later heads need to know 'what came just before me', most famously for induction.
hamming.why: Attention is the only way information moves between positions, and many later tricks depend on this one-step relay existing.

object.title: The pegboard of glances
object.subtitle: Each row of pegs is one word; the tall peg marks where it looked. Slide the stripe to meet different kinds of head.

cap.1: Each row of pegs is one word, and the tall peg shows where it looked. Every word looks exactly one step back.
cap.2: An 8x8 attention pattern: rows are destinations, columns are sources. This is a previous-token head.
cap.3: A[i, i−1] ≈ 1: the sub-diagonal, with position 0 falling back to BOS.

cap.1: From above, the tall pegs form a stripe one step below the diagonal: the fingerprint to look for.
cap.2: The detector averages that sub-diagonal. A high score marks a candidate previous-token head.
cap.3: Score = mean of A.diagonal(−1); the causal mask keeps everything above the diagonal empty.

cap.1: Slide the stripe onto the diagonal and each word looks only at itself. A different kind of head.
cap.2: Offset 0 is a current-token head. Same detector, different diagonal.
cap.3: The offset selects the circuit: 0 current-token, −1 previous-token, 1 − seq_len induction on repeated text.

cap.1: Look three back and the early words, with nobody that far in front, pile onto the start marker.
cap.2: In this toy, positions with no i−3 fall back to BOS, a common resting place for spare attention.
cap.3: The toy routes out-of-range glances to BOS; real heads often park attention there when their target is absent.

cap.1: The peg only shows where a word looked. The note it writes matters only when a later head reads it.
cap.2: Patterns show where a head looks, not whether it matters. Patching tells you that.
cap.3: Attention patterns are QK-side evidence; the causal role (an OV write read by later keys) needs ablation or patching.

predict.q: Where does a previous-token head's bright stripe sit in its attention pattern?

options.t: One step below the main diagonal

predict.why: Row i (destination) puts its attention on column i−1 (source): the sub-diagonal. The main diagonal is a current-token head.

predict.q: DLA gives your previous-token head a score near zero. Is it unimportant?

options.t: Not necessarily: its effect runs through later heads
Yes: it does not move the logits

predict.why: DLA only sees direct paths. The prev-token head works indirectly, by feeding induction heads' keys.

predict.q: You zero-ablate head 0.7 in ARENA's 2-layer model. What happens on repeated random text?

options.t: Loss on the second copy climbs back up
Nothing: the layer-1 heads manage alone

predict.why: The induction heads need the note 0.7 writes. Without it they no longer know where to look.

object.where: Anywhere a value is passed one step along a sequence: shift registers, causal convolutions, the first half of induction.
